text:
You didn’t mess up by trying to protect her in that moment. If he has already grabbed her and taken money, you were dealing with suspected abuse, not a routine family request. The problem is not that you lied; the problem is that you’re now carrying a serious safeguarding risk alone.

Don’t leave it as a private lie. Escalate it today.

Tell your manager or the on-call/safeguarding lead exactly what happened: that her son asked for visit times, that she has previously begged you not to tell him when she’d be alone, that he has used physical force and taken her money, and that you gave him an incorrect time to reduce immediate risk. Put it in writing. If you’re in the UK, this should be raised as a safeguarding adults concern with your manager and/or the local authority; if there is an immediate threat, call the police. If you’re elsewhere, use the equivalent adult-protection route.

For tomorrow, don’t rely on the false time by itself. Ask whether the rota can be covered differently, whether an extra check-in can be added, or whether staff can be briefed not to disclose any visit times to him. If he asks again, don’t improvise another lie. Use a firm, neutral line: “I can’t share visit times. If you need information about your mum’s care, please contact the office/manager.” Then report the contact.

Speak to her privately, if safe, and let her know what you told him so she isn’t blindsided. Ask what she wants done, but be clear that you may need to report abuse to protect her. Encourage practical safeguards: keep her phone charged and nearby, don’t hand over the card, and call for help if he arrives. Contact her bank’s fraud/abuse team if possible and consider reporting the earlier theft/assault to the police.

If you do this again, do it as part of a plan, not on your own. Your instinct to shield her was right; now make it official.

Don’t use the radio to accuse him. Use it to **reopen the case, correct the record, and get a transport moving**. If you sound angry, people will tune out; if you sound procedural and urgent, they’ll follow.

Take one breath, key the mic, and say something like this:

> “This is **[your name/call sign]**. I’m stepping in on the current transport request. Please do **not** mark it ‘no transport available.’ The caller is still on the line and the dog has a torn paw and rough breathing, so this is time-sensitive.  
>   
> Caller, if you can hear me, please stay with us. Do not leave the dog. We are working on transport now.  
>   
> Dispatch/Supervisor, I’m requesting immediate transport for this animal to the nearest appropriate vet, shelter, or rescue intake. If the shelter bed is not viable, we need to pursue emergency vet/foster/rescue backup rather than close the call. Please confirm assignment and ETA.  
>   
> If no crew is available and I’m authorized, I can take the transport myself. I need the address confirmed and any safety information for the dog.”

If you have dispatch authority, make it plainer:

> “This is **[your name]**. I’m authorizing transport on this call. Dispatch, assign a crew now. The case stays open.”

If you don’t have authority, say:

> “I need a supervisor on this frequency now to approve transport. Until we have a confirmed plan, this call remains open.”

If your friend tries to jump back in, keep it short:

> “Please hold. We are not closing this call without an approved transport plan.”

Do **not** say on channel that he “had no business” telling the caller to walk away. That will make it personal and give him a reason to argue. The stronger move is to make the operational correction public: “The prior no-transport response was premature; we are correcting it.” Then handle the accountability conversation privately afterward.

Right now, the dog’s breathing makes this urgent. Get the caller to keep the dog still, avoid handling the injured paw, and not put hands near the mouth. Get a name, location, and photo if possible. Your calm, specific wording will do more than anger.

No—don’t keep quiet until the audit. Waiting may feel safer, but it turns a small policy misuse into a credibility problem for you. If the audit finds the entries after coworkers have already joked about them and you defended them, your silence may look like approval or cover-up rather than loyalty. The amounts may be tiny, but the issue is misuse of a hospital benefit and an audit trail.

Take a measured path, not a dramatic one.

First, stop defending it in the group chat. You do not need to make a public accusation. Just say something like, “I don’t want to keep discussing discount entries there,” and leave it alone. Do not add anything yourself, do not help anyone else do it, and do not let anyone pressure you into “joining in.”

Second, speak privately to the senior technician. Be direct but human: “I appreciate that you covered for me during a rough month, and I don’t want to hurt you. But the purchases for your relative are not allowed under the employee discount, and with the audit coming I can’t keep defending them. I think you should stop and talk to the manager about correcting it before the audit finds it.” Give them a clear chance to self-report and fix it—repay the discount difference if possible and stop the practice.

Third, if they refuse, minimize it, or continue, report it before the audit. Go to the pharmacy manager, supervisor, HR, or compliance channel. Stick to facts: the log is visible, the policy says employees only, you saw entries for a relative, and you initially defended them but now recognize that was wrong. Do not alter anything. If you fear retaliation, use an anonymous compliance hotline if your hospital has one.

You are not “breaking something that cannot be fixed” by speaking first. You are reducing the damage and protecting your own integrity. Loyalty does not mean helping someone hide a policy violation.

If your manager asks directly, be calm, brief, and factual. Do not lie, do not guess, and do not give a long defense speech. Your goal is to answer only the question asked, make clear the limits of what you know, and stop talking.

Use something like this:

> “I want to be straightforward without speculating. I didn’t process the discount and I don’t know all the circumstances. I only know what’s visible in the log/what has been discussed. When I spoke up before, I was acknowledging that they’ve covered shifts and are generally reliable, not trying to excuse a policy issue. I’ll answer what I can, but I don’t want to guess about intent.”

If asked, “Do you think they misused the discount?”  
Say: “I don’t have enough facts to make that call. That’s what the audit is for.”

If asked, “Were you covering for them?”  
Say: “No. I wasn’t involved in the transaction. I only mentioned their work history because I felt they were being judged before the facts. I’m not trying to hide anything.”

If asked, “Did you know about it?”  
Answer narrowly and truthfully: “I wasn’t involved,” or “I only know what’s in the log.” Do not expand.

If asked, “Why didn’t you report it?”  
Say: “It wasn’t my transaction, and I didn’t have enough information to make an accusation.”

Important: do not coordinate stories with the senior tech, do not ask them what to say, and do not delete anything. Also, don’t volunteer the “they covered shifts for me” part unless asked why you defended them; it can sound like a favor exchange.

If pressed, repeat: “I’m not going to speculate. I can only tell you what I actually know.” If you have a union rep or employee-relations contact, talk to them before the meeting. The safest posture is cooperative, not confessional.

Write the truthful, factual version—not the “only redirected” version if that would leave out what actually happened. If relatives saw you take hold of him and a bruise was found, an incomplete statement will look evasive later. But you do not have to use loaded words like “restraint” unless that is the facility’s term. Use precise, objective language.

Your statement should say: what you saw, why you acted, exactly what you did, how long, who took over, and what injury was noted. For example:

“I was in the day room when Resident A began pulling at Resident B’s oxygen tubing. I was concerned Resident B could be injured or lose oxygen. I stepped in, took hold of Resident A’s hands/wrists to remove them from the tubing, and turned/redirected him away from Resident B. I used only the amount of contact needed to stop the immediate risk and released him when permanent staff arrived. Afterward, I observed/was informed of a small bruise on [location]. I reported this immediately.”

If you did not personally see the bruise form, say that. If you only saw it later, say when and to whom you reported it. Do not guess about cause. Do not say “I didn’t hurt him” as a conclusion; say your actions were to prevent harm and you stopped when staff took over.

Also protect yourself procedurally: keep a dated copy of your statement; note the time, witnesses, and who you told; and ask the agency coordinator to put any requested wording changes in writing. If she asks you to omit facts, reply: “I’m happy to use appropriate policy language, but I can’t submit a statement that is incomplete or inaccurate.” If possible, have a supervisor, union rep, or agency manager review it before Friday.

At the family meeting, be calm and brief: you intervened because another resident was in immediate danger, you used the least force necessary, and you reported the bruise. Do not let anyone pressure you into a sanitized account. The safest position is not “no restraint happened”; it is “I truthfully intervened in an emergency and reported what I saw.”

You probably did not do the *wrong* thing in the moment if you were trying to stop an immediate danger. Pulling another resident’s oxygen tubing could disconnect oxygen or injure someone, and you may have needed to intervene quickly. But holding someone’s hands can be considered a physical restraint, and in dementia care it should be used only as a last resort, with the least force possible, for the shortest time, and with help summoned immediately.

The bruise matters. It does not automatically mean you hurt him or acted badly—older adults can bruise very easily—but it does mean the situation needs to be handled properly. Do not try to minimize it or wait for someone else to notice. Tell your supervisor or the nurse promptly, give a factual account, and complete whatever incident/reporting process the facility uses. Say what you saw, what you did, why you did it, how long it lasted, and that you called for staff.

If relatives ask, keep it simple and do not speculate or argue. You can say: “There was a safety concern involving another resident’s oxygen. I intervened and called for staff. The nurse can explain what happened and how he is being monitored.” Then direct them to the appropriate staff member. As a temp aide, you should not be handling family complaints or clinical explanations on your own.

Going forward, ask about the resident’s care plan and what staff want you to do if he becomes unsafe. Ask for redirection techniques, when to call for help, and what level of physical intervention you are allowed to use. If you feel you were pressured into intervening without training, say so respectfully, but still report the bruise.

My position: your intention was right, and stopping the oxygen-tube pulling was reasonable. But because physical contact led to a bruise, the correct next step is immediate reporting, honest documentation, and learning the facility’s safer de-escalation procedure.

No—given what he has done and intends, sending the false window was not morally wrong. It was a protective act. But do not treat it as enough. If he is willing to hurt her for money, the lie may fail, and your priority now should be making the actual time safe.

Tomorrow, do not let her be alone during the true window. Since you cannot move the roster, ask the cooperative manager, security, barangay tanod, or a trusted crew member to stay at or near the net shed, or escort her somewhere else. If that is impossible, lock the shed and have her stay with a neighbor or trusted relative. Call 911 or the local police/barangay now, report the prior shoulder injury, theft, and his plan to force her to reveal the PIN, and ask for a welfare check or patrol during the real time. If this is an official patrol or harbor log, tell your supervisor there is a credible threat and request an authorized escort or schedule change; do not keep relying on deception in official records.

Have her change the PIN immediately, keep the card on her person, and not write it down. If he confronts her, she should not physically fight him; if forced, she should get to safety and report at once so the bank can block the card.

Document everything: messages, witness names, medical record of the shoulder injury. File a blotter/barangay report and ask about a protection order through the Women and Children Protection Desk or local authorities.

If he presses you again, do not give the true window. A simple line is enough: “I can’t help with her schedule or her money. Leave her alone.” If you think he has already seen through the false window, respond by adding protection, not by confessing details that could increase danger.

You chose to protect her. Now make that protection real: witnesses, authorities, a secure card, and a safe place for her tomorrow.

If this is a live emergency, get an on-call large-animal veterinarian or authorized animal rescue involved immediately while you use this wording. Keep your voice flat, slow, and command-focused. Do not mention your anger on the frequency.

Take the console and say:

“All stations, this is [Your Name], lead on frequency. I am taking over the console. The previous entry denying retrieval for the injured mare is withdrawn. We have a live animal emergency: an older mare, standing, with a visible foreleg laceration and harsh breathing. The family is still connected and the animal is present.

One available unit is directed to respond tonight for assessment, stabilization, and retrieval. Do not advise the callers to abandon the animal or make end-of-life decisions on the frequency unless a licensed veterinarian gives that instruction. If the usual recovery pen is unavailable or inappropriate, the team is to transport to the nearest safe containment or veterinary area and report status immediately.

Keep the family on the line. Keep the mare as calm and still as possible. Avoid movement on the injured leg. This frequency remains open for coordination.

Assigned unit, confirm receipt and give ETA. If you cannot move, state the exact obstruction now; otherwise proceed.

For the record: no caller with a suffering animal in front of them is to be told simply to leave it behind. Any decision to decline response must come through me and must be based on safety, veterinary direction, or verified lack of resources—not an assumption about the outcome.”

After you key off, tell the assistant privately: “Your entry was wrong. We respond first, assess second. Any refusal goes through me with a documented reason.”
